title: The Roofline Model
summary: Diagnosing whether a workload is compute-bound or memory-bound before spending time optimizing it.

slides.subTitle: Compute-bound or memory-bound?
slides.markdown:
Before optimizing a piece of numerical code, you need to know **what's actually limiting it**: is the CPU/GPU's raw compute throughput the bottleneck, or is it waiting on data to arrive from memory? Optimizing the wrong one wastes effort entirely.

The **roofline model** answers this visually — it plots a workload's achievable performance against a hardware's compute and memory-bandwidth limits, making the bottleneck a matter of "which line is this workload sitting under" rather than guesswork.

slides.subTitle: FLOPs per byte moved
slides.markdown:
**Arithmetic intensity** = FLOPs performed ÷ bytes moved from memory. It's the single number that places a workload on the roofline plot's x-axis.

A workload doing a huge amount of computation per byte fetched (high intensity) can afford to be limited by compute throughput, since memory traffic is comparatively small. A workload that fetches a lot of data but does little math per byte (low intensity) is far more likely to be capped by how fast bytes can arrive, not by how fast the ALU can crunch them.

slides.subTitle: Two ceilings, one graph
slides.markdown:
The roofline overlays two hardware limits on one chart.

![A roofline plot with a compute ceiling and a memory-bandwidth slope, with a workload point placed](assets/roofline-plot.svg)

The flat line is peak compute throughput — a ceiling independent of intensity. The diagonal line is peak memory bandwidth translated into achievable FLOPs — it rises with intensity, since more compute per byte means bandwidth constrains you less.

assets.alt: A roofline plot with a compute ceiling and a memory-bandwidth slope, with a workload point placed

slides.subTitle: Under the slope, or under the flat line
slides.markdown:
Plot your workload's arithmetic intensity and achieved performance as one point. Under the **diagonal** (memory-bandwidth) line: **memory-bound** — it hits the bandwidth ceiling before the compute ceiling. Under the **flat** (compute) line at high intensity: **compute-bound** — bandwidth was never the constraint.

The point's horizontal position (intensity) is a property of the algorithm; its vertical position is what you're trying to raise — the ceiling directly above it tells you which lever to pull.

slides.subTitle: Different regions, different fixes
slides.markdown:
If you're **memory-bound**, adding more compute throughput (wider vector units, more cores) does nothing — the bottleneck is bytes per second, not FLOPs per second. You need to move less data, or move it more efficiently (better locality, compression, fusing operations to reuse data already in registers/cache).

If you're **compute-bound**, more memory bandwidth is wasted money — you need more raw compute throughput, or a way to do the same math in fewer operations (algorithmic improvement, better use of SIMD/vector units).

slides.subTitle: A dot product
slides.markdown:
```text
Dot product of two length-N float32 vectors:
  FLOPs   = N multiplies + N adds = 2N
  Bytes   = 2 vectors x N elements x 4 bytes = 8N

Arithmetic intensity = 2N / 8N = 0.25 FLOPs/byte
```

That's a very low intensity — a dot product does almost no math relative to the data it streams through, which is exactly why it's a textbook memory-bound kernel: no amount of extra compute throughput speeds it up until memory bandwidth is addressed first.

slides.subTitle: Memory-bound vs compute-bound fixes
slides.markdown:
| Bound by | Example fix | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Memory bandwidth | Cache blocking/tiling (cross-link: cache-conscious-programming) | Reuses data already fetched instead of re-streaming it from memory |
| Compute throughput | Vectorization / SIMD (cross-link: multicore -> simd-and-vector-processing) | Does more arithmetic per instruction issued, raising the achievable-FLOPs ceiling |

**How to decide:** the roofline point tells you which fix applies — cache blocking helps a memory-bound point by effectively raising its arithmetic intensity (same FLOPs, fewer bytes actually fetched from memory), while vectorization helps a compute-bound point by raising the compute ceiling itself. Applying the wrong one (e.g. vectorizing a memory-bound kernel) buys little to nothing.

slides.subTitle: The exact arithmetic intensity where the two ceilings cross
slides.markdown:
The **ridge point** is the arithmetic intensity where the memory-bandwidth line meets the compute ceiling — the boundary between memory-bound and compute-bound territory for a given piece of hardware.

```
peak compute      = 20 TFLOP/s
peak bandwidth    = 800 GB/s

ridge point = peak_compute / peak_bandwidth
            = 20e12 / 800e9
            = 25 FLOPs/byte
```

A workload with arithmetic intensity below 25 FLOPs/byte on this hardware is memory-bound no matter how well-optimized its compute is; above 25, it's compute-bound no matter how much memory bandwidth is available. The dot product from the earlier worked example (0.25 FLOPs/byte) sits **100x below** this ridge point — deeply memory-bound — while a dense matrix multiply (arithmetic intensity that scales with matrix dimension, often reaching hundreds of FLOPs/byte for large matrices) comfortably clears it and becomes compute-bound. The ridge point is a property of the *hardware*; where your workload's intensity falls relative to it is what actually determines which ceiling to attack.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: matrix multiply's much higher intensity
slides.subTitle: Why matmul tolerates optimization that a dot product can't
slides.markdown:
Multiplying two NxN matrices (naive triple-loop): each output element does N multiply-adds, and there are N^2 output elements.

```
FLOPs = N^2 outputs * 2N ops each = 2N^3
Bytes (naive, re-reading rows/columns from memory each time) ~ O(N^3) as well if there's no reuse

with good cache blocking (tiling), each matrix element is loaded once per tile
and reused many times within on-chip cache:
Bytes (blocked) ~ O(N^3 / B)  where B is roughly the tile size

arithmetic intensity (blocked) = 2N^3 / (N^3/B) = 2B FLOPs/byte
```

With a tile size B of, say, 64, that's roughly 128 FLOPs/byte — comfortably above a typical hardware ridge point (like the 25 FLOPs/byte from the previous slide), landing matmul in compute-bound territory *if* it's tiled well. An un-tiled, naive matmul implementation can still be memory-bound despite doing the exact same total FLOPs — the arithmetic intensity depends on how the code is written, not just what math it computes, which is exactly why cache blocking is one of the highest-leverage optimizations in numerical computing.
